# Runner config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/runners/<stem>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.RunnerBlock` (ADR-106 D1) declaring one **runner** — a machine that is not the daemon's, running `tera runner`, holding one long-lived outbound link to this daemon and executing tool dispatches locally. A `recipe`-regime kind (ADR-087 D3 Amendment 7): one runner per file, the filename stem is the identity, and a block label that disagrees with the stem is a hard error rather than a silent rewrite.

**The credential is admin-tier, and the block's smallness is not a guide to its weight.** A runner is admitted by the lowercase-hex SHA-256 of a bearer key only its host holds, and the declaration never states it: the hash is daemon state, kept in this daemon's runner record (ADR-165 D4). On the golden path the host joins by a join line (`tera runners install-line <name>`), mints its own key at enrolment and sends only the hash. A host installed with no join token — on a daemon whose runner listeners are all plaintext, say — is admitted by hand: its install prints the key's hash, and `tera runners adopt <name> --hash <sha256>` records it. `api_key_hash` is refused by name at load, `tera config validate`, plan and apply, and the refusal names that repair. A holder of the matching key attaches as this runner and is handed tool dispatches to execute — which is permission to run arbitrary sandboxed code on that host, under that host's own OS credentials, reaching whatever that host's keychain and egress allow-list reach (ADR-106 D8). It is **not** a worker-tier grant and must not be documented as one. A recorded key is replaced by `tera runners rotate`, with no step on the host; a key that may have been read by someone else is revoked, `tera runners revoke`, not rotated.

**The name is the host id.** The label is both the declaration's name and the id the runner must advertise on connect — a runner that authenticates under this declaration and advertises a different id is refused at advertisement, before the link settles, so a leaked key cannot claim to be a different machine. Collapsing the two into one name is what makes that checkable without a second field that could be left blank or drift from the name every other surface uses.

**What the block deliberately does not carry.** No address, no port, no transport: a runner *dials the daemon*, so the daemon never needs to reach it and an operator never states where it is — which is what makes a laptop behind NAT a first-class fleet host. And no capability list: what a runner can serve is a fact about that machine — does the handler binary resolve, does the toolchain exist, is the named credential present in *this* keychain — so it is advertised by the runner at connect and on every reconnect, never declared here. A declared list would be an operator's guess about a machine they are not standing on, and it would go stale in silence.

`enabled` is the off switch, and unset means enabled: a declared runner is admitted by its credential. `enabled = false` refuses its link and a join token for it, and leaves its credential where it is, so taking a machine out of rotation for an hour changes no credential. Deleting the declaration is not a revocation: a credential this daemon recorded is kept and admits again when the name is declared again, and only `tera runners revoke` removes it.

**One label is reserved, and declaring it is how the daemon joins a pool.** `runner "local"` is this daemon's own host (ADR-133 D1). It is written BOUNDS-ONLY — `description`, `seats`, `serves`, and `state` with its `reason`, and nothing else — because it runs in this daemon's own process and is never dialled: there is no key for anything to present, and an `api_key_hash` here is refused, since a digest would admit a REMOTE claimant under the name of this machine. `enabled` is refused too, and for a different reason: whether this daemon executes at all is the tool-dispatch posture, which is kernel-owned and restart-bound (ADR-122 D2, unchanged by ADR-133 D7), so write `mode = "remote_only"` in the bootstrap kernel to take this host out of execution, or `seats = 0` here for a ceiling of zero, which admits nothing while it stays a declared machine.

Declaring it is what lets an ordinary admission-only `member "local" {}` name the daemon in a DECLARED pool — by either road to one, a `runner_link.default_host_pool` or a worker's own `seat_pools`. Without it the daemon's host is a placement target only where no host pool is named at all, because a declared default replaces the implicit fleet deployment-wide (D4). Its ceiling resolves through the same `config.MemberCeiling` join every other machine's does, so `member "local" { seats = … }` beside it is refused with the same sentence. Under `mode = "remote_only"` the whole authoring is refused, naming the posture.

**`seats` is this machine's concurrency ceiling** (ADR-133 D4), with three distinct states spelled exactly as a pool member's `seats` spells them: `0` is a ceiling of zero (declared and admitted, admitting nothing because it can hold nothing — a statement about capacity, not a drain, ADR-178 D7), `n` bounds it at n, and unset is unbounded. It lives here rather than on a pool `member` because a ceiling is a fact about the machine: an implicit fleet has no member file to carry one, and a member's `seats` is shared across every pool that lists it, so one machine could otherwise carry two different ceilings depending on which pool drew. A member whose name matches a declared runner and which also states `seats` is refused — there is one home, not two — and the refusal names the repair and `docs/ops/upgrade-to-seat-admitted-execution.md`.

**`state` and `reason` say whether this machine takes work** (ADR-178 D1, D3), in every pool its member is in and in the implicit fleet. `open`, the default and what an unset `state` means, admits new placements and pinned resumes — runs whose workspace is on this machine — within `seats`; `draining` refuses new placements and still admits pinned resumes; `closed` refuses both. No state stops work already running on the machine or changes its link: a draining or closed runner stays connected, reports, takes rollouts and finishes what it holds. `draining` and `closed` require a `reason` saying why, and an empty or whitespace-only one is refused; a `reason` beside an open machine is refused, because it would describe a state the machine is not in (D4). Both are legal on every declaration, `runner "local"` included, and `seats` keeps its value whatever the state, so reopening is deleting the two lines. **The seat gate admits by the state**: a draining or closed machine takes no new work in any pool, and a pool with no open member refuses new work with the cause `not-open`. A resume pinned to a closed machine is refused in every pool with the cause `workspace-pin-closed`: the run is held for the machine while the worker's `workspace_hold_deadline` runs, past which it is placed on another machine and its session is lost, and reopening the machine before then resumes the run on it.

**A `class {}` block makes the declaration a class** (ADR-165 D5): `runner "builders" { class { max_members = 20 } }` stands for hosts nobody names. Each host that enrols with a join token minted for it is a **member**, admitted under an identity of its own fixed at enrolment, which advertises the class's name — so on a class the label is the declaration its members answer to, not any member's identity. `max_members` is required and positive. What the rest of the block carries, a class carries for each member: `seats` is each member's ceiling, `host {}` each member's runner-level policy, `enabled = false` refuses every member, `rollout { hold }` holds every member, and `state` with its `reason` is every member's state. A class takes no `api_key_hash`, because its members are admitted by enrolment, and `runner "local"` takes no `class {}`. The members are daemon state, never configuration. Without the block the declaration is a named runner, exactly as above.

Status: **preview**.

## Example

A minimal `runners`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/runners/example-runner.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

runner "example-runner" {
  description = "What this is for, in one line."
  seats       = 1
}
```

## Attributes

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | yes | — | — | block label | Runner name. It is also the host id this runner must advertise on connect — a runner that authenticates under this declaration and advertises a different id is refused, so a leaked key cannot claim to be a different machine. On a class (a declaration with a class {} block) the name is the DECLARATION its members advertise, not any member's identity: each member is admitted under an identity of its own, fixed at enrolment, and advertises this name (ADR-165 D6). Under the recipe identity regime it must equal the file stem. |
| `description` | string | no | — | — | — | Operator prose. The only place this block records which physical machine it means — there is deliberately no address, since a runner dials out. |
| `class` | block | no | — | ADR-165 D5 ([W4-C1]) | — | Makes this declaration a CLASS: one declaration standing for hosts nobody names (ADR-165 D5). Present, the declaration is a class and each host that enrols with a join token minted for it (tera runners install-line <name>) is admitted as a member, under an identity of its own fixed at enrolment, and advertises this declaration's name. Absent, the declaration is a named runner — one machine, whose identity is this name. What the rest of this block carries, a class carries for EACH member: seats is each member's ceiling, host {} is each member's runner-level policy, enabled = false refuses every member, rollout { hold } holds every member, and state with its reason is every member's state. A member "<name>" {} in a pool admits every member of the class. A class takes no api_key_hash, because its members are admitted by enrolment. Refused on runner "local". The members themselves are daemon state, never configuration. |
| `api_key_hash` | string | no | — | — | — | Refused, whatever its value: a runner's credential is daemon state, kept in this daemon's runner record and never in a vault (ADR-165 D4). A host joins by a join line (tera runners install-line <name>), whose enrolment records its key's hash; a host installed with no join token is admitted by tera runners adopt <name> --hash <sha256>, with the hash its install printed. A runner once admitted by this attribute keeps its key: remove the attribute, apply, and adopt the value with --hash unless tera runners list shows it already recorded. Declared, the attribute is refused by name at load, tera config validate, plan and apply, and the refusal names that repair. The hash it named is admin-tier: the matching key is permission to execute arbitrary sandboxed code on that host with that host's own credentials (ADR-106 D8). |
| `seats` | integer | no | — | — | — | Concurrent-dispatch ceiling for this machine. Three distinct states, spelled exactly as a pool member's seats spells them: seats = 0 is a ceiling of ZERO (declared and admitted, admitting nothing because it can hold nothing — a statement about capacity, not a drain, ADR-178 D7); seats = n bounds it at n; unset is UNBOUNDED, which is what local execution is today. Unset is not a synonym for 0 and not a synonym for any n. The ceiling lives here rather than on a pool member because it is a fact about the machine: an implicit fleet has no member file to carry it, and a member's seats is shared across every pool that lists it, so one machine could otherwise carry two ceilings (ADR-133 D4). A member naming a declared runner and also stating seats is refused — there is one home, not two. On a class, seats is EACH MEMBER'S ceiling, not the class's total (ADR-133 D4 as amended by ADR-165 D5): a class of 20 with seats = 4 is 20 machines of 4 seats each. |
| `state` | string | no | `open` | ADR-178 D3 (PLAN-2026-10 member-state, Wave 1) | — | This machine's state (ADR-178 D1, D3), in EVERY pool this machine's member is in and in the implicit fleet. open, the default and what unset means, admits new placements and pinned resumes within seats; draining refuses new placements and still admits pinned resumes (runs whose workspace is on this machine) within seats; closed refuses both. No state stops, interrupts or reclaims work already running on the machine, and none changes its link: a draining or closed runner stays connected, reports, takes rollouts and finishes what it holds. Legal on every runner declaration, runner "local" included, beside description, seats and serves. On a class (a declaration with a class {} block) the state applies to EVERY MEMBER of the class. seats keeps its value whatever the state, so reopening is deleting state and reason, or writing state = "open". Any other value is refused. The seat gate admits by the state: a draining or closed machine takes no new work in any pool, and a pool with no open member refuses new work with the cause not-open. A resume pinned to a closed machine is refused in every pool with the cause workspace-pin-closed: the run is held for the machine while the worker's workspace_hold_deadline runs, past which it is placed on another machine and its session is lost. A closed runner "local" is the exception: a run pinned to the daemon's own host is held until it reopens, with no deadline, because that machine is never away. Reopening the machine while the run is held resumes the run on it. |
| `reason` | string | no | — | ADR-178 D3 (PLAN-2026-10 member-state, Wave 1) | — | Why this machine is draining or closed (ADR-178 D4). Required when state is draining or closed, and an empty or whitespace-only reason is refused: a machine left out of rotation that nobody can explain is the failure this attribute exists to prevent. Refused when state is open or unset, because it would describe a state the machine is not in. On a class it is the reason for every member. |
| `serves` | string[] | no | — | ADR-133 D15 ([W3-C3b]) | — | Narrows what this daemon's own host offers to a seat draw. LEGAL ON runner "local" AND NOWHERE ELSE — a machine that dials advertises its own offer at connect and is refused this attribute, because a declared list about a machine you are not standing on goes stale silently (ADR-133 D3). Unset means this host offers whatever its handlers resolve, which is what mode = "local" has always meant and what every deployment that declares nothing gets. A declared list ONLY EVER NARROWS: it takes names out of that offer, so the local host is excluded from a draw for a capability it does not list, and the dispatch goes to a machine that does offer it or is refused at the draw naming the capability. There is no value of this attribute that makes this host offer something it otherwise would not — it is read through the offer port, whose local arm can answer "does not offer" and never "offers". This is what platform { tool_dispatch { local_capabilities } } retired into (ADR-133 D7/D15), and it is NOT a rename: the old set was a widening beneath a remote_only posture, this is a narrowing under a permitting one, and it draws a seat where the old set did not. An EMPTY list is refused rather than read as either "no narrowing" or "nothing" — a host that offers nothing is seats = 0. Names match the REGISTERED capability name exactly, on the same terms the retired attribute used: a system-vault tool bare ("uuidv7") or namespaced ("system/tools/uuidv7"), a user vault's only as "<vault-id>/tools/<stem>". Hot-reloads, like every other runner attribute. |
| `host` | block | no | — | — | — | This runner's own host policy (ADR-164 D2): the same block, with the same fields, as runner_link { host {} }, where each field is documented. A field declared here wins over the fleet's for this machine alone, field by field; a field not declared here takes the fleet's. Refused on runner "local": the daemon's own host takes no host policy, because its runner uses the daemon's own stores, which platform {} bounds. Hot-reloadable. |
| `rollout` | block | no | — | — | — | This runner's part in its fleet's rollouts (ADR-163 D10.3). Its one attribute, hold, keeps the runner on its build until it is removed, and is a reason rather than a boolean. Refused on runner "local". Hot-reloadable. |
| `enabled` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Whether this runner may connect. Unset means enabled: a declared runner is admitted by the credential this daemon recorded for it. Set false to refuse its link and a join token for it while its credential stays as it is, so taking a machine out of rotation changes no credential. Deleting the declaration is not a revocation: a recorded credential is kept and admits again when the name is declared again, and only tera runners revoke removes it. |

## `class` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `max_members` | integer | yes | — | ADR-165 D5 ([W4-C1]) | — | The most hosts this class may hold as enrolled members at once (ADR-165 D5.2). Required, and a positive integer: an unbounded class with a join token is a door held open. The bound counts every enrolled member, connected or not; a revoked member does not count, so revoking one frees its place. An enrolment past the bound is refused naming it, and tera runners install-line refuses to mint a token for a class that is full. Lowering it below the current count evicts nobody: the class reads as over its bound, and every further enrolment is refused until members are revoked. Hot-reloadable. |

## `rollout` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `hold` | string | no | — | — | — | Keeps this runner on its build across every rollout until the attribute is removed, and says why (ADR-163 D10.3). A hold is a reason, not a boolean: the text is shown wherever the hold is, and an empty or whitespace-only one is refused, because a host left behind that nobody can explain is the failure this attribute exists to prevent. Unset means the runner is rolled with its fleet. Refused on runner "local": this daemon's own host follows the daemon and is never rolled. Hot-reloadable. |
